column1: # Requirements for Mica::Form: the WHATWG URL Standard's
# (section 5.2), the web-platform-tests vectors for them, Mica's bracket and
# dot key grammar for Mica::Form::NestedKeys (no standard defines it; the
# grammar is documented on the class), and Mica's form hardening.

column3: Input is split on 0x26 (&) into sequences
Empty sequences produce no pair
A sequence splits at its first 0x3D (=); without one the whole sequence is the name and the value is empty
0x2B (+) in the name and value becomes 0x20 (space)
%XX with two hex digits decodes to its byte; any other % stays as it is

column2: WHATWG URL 5.1 step 3.5 UTF-8 decode without BOM
column3: Decoded bytes are UTF-8 and a leading BOM is kept; Mica rejects invalid UTF-8 with EncodingError instead of substituting U+FFFD
Pairs keep input order and repeated names
The serializer percent-encodes with the urlencoded set, writes space as +, and joins pairs with = and &
Every web-platform-tests urlencoded parser vector passes, or is rejected by the strict UTF-8 policy at the predicted byte
The web-platform-tests stringifier expectations hold for the serializer
A key without [ (and without . under dot notation) is one hash key
Under dot notation a key without [ splits at dots into hash keys; with dot notation off it stays one key
An empty part between dots raises KeySyntaxError
The head is the bytes before the first [ and must not be empty
After the head only complete [..] segments may follow; anything else raises KeySyntaxError
A canonical decimal segment is an array index; any other segment is a hash key
[] as the last segment appends the value
[] before a hash key continues the last hash unless it already holds the rest of the key (Rack rule)
[] before an index or another [] starts a new array
Sparse indices are stored sparsely and the result is dense with nil slots
A key needing a different kind of value than the one already at its path raises KeyConflictError
A repeated string path keeps the last value, or raises KeyConflictError under DuplicateLeaves::Reject
Hash keys keep first-seen order
Amber's nested parameter fixtures give the same structure (strings, before type coercion)
Key errors carry the byte offset of the offending pair in the original input
Every form entry point takes a required limits argument; unbounded limits need a non-blank reason
Input longer than max_input_bytes raises LimitExceededError at byte max_input_bytes, from bytes and from streams
More than max_pairs pairs raises LimitExceededError at the first extra pair
A key with more than max_key_depth segments raises LimitExceededError
An array index or append above max_array_index raises LimitExceededError without allocating
Array slots in the whole result are capped by max_array_slots
The work budget stops a parse with WorkBudgetExceededError
An expired deadline stops a parse with DeadlineExceededError
Invalid UTF-8 raises EncodingError at the input byte where the invalid sequence starts, for every hostile byte class
A String, Bytes and a trickling IO give identical pairs and identical errors
Pair parsing is linear: many separators, long percent runs, many plus signs
Key mapping is linear: huge indices are O(1), deep keys are bounded, many keys and append chains stay linear
Seeded hostile fuzzing finds no crash, overrun, nondeterminism or stream disagreement
Pairs agree with stdlib URI::Params wherever both accept valid UTF-8 input
